title: Insertion and Selection Sort
summary: The simple quadratic sorts and what they teach - selection sort, insertion sort and why it is fast on nearly sorted data, inversions as a measure of disorder, stability, sorting in place, comparators and strict weak ordering, and why real libraries still use insertion sort for small pieces.

cards.a:
2

(3, 1) and (3, 2) are out of order; (1, 2) is fine.

cards.q: On an already sorted array of n elements, how much work does insertion sort do?
cards.a:
O(n)

Each element is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put. Insertion sort does n plus the number of inversions, and a sorted array has none.

cards.q: Why must a comparator use < rather than <=?
cards.a:
less(a, a) must be false, and <= breaks that

The sort requires a strict weak ordering. With <=, equal elements each claim to be less than the other, which can make std::sort misbehave or crash.
